## Daily average sea surface temperature from buoys -- climatologies and anomalies

```{r setup}
load_all()    # for developer
# library(pacea)  # for user
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)  # Else prints all of a tibble
library(ggplot2)
```

In pacea we include daily average sea surface temperature (SST) that we have calculated from
two-minute measurements from `r nrow(buoy_metadata)` buoys in
Canadian Pacific waters, yielding over 200,000 daily means.
Data are from Environment and Climate Change Canada, and Fisheries and
Oceans Canada. The earliest data are from September 1987, and 18 buoys were
still providing data as of August 2026.

See the
[buoys_vignette](https://pbs-assess.github.io/pacea/vignettes/buoys.html) and
the help file `?buoy_sst` 
for background concerning the calculated daily mean sea surface temperatures
and associated simple plotting functions in pacea. Here we focus on
constructing climatologies and subsequent anomalies, to plot in 
a standardised way.

The locations of the buoys are:
```{r buoysmap, echo=FALSE, fig.width = 5.7, fig.height = 5, out.width = "90%"}
knitr::include_graphics(paste0(here::here(),
                               "/man/figures/buoys_map.png"))
```

If you want to quickly get a sense of current temperatures (and aso across the wider
  northeast Pacific Ocean), check out Andrea Hilborn et al.'s
  [Pacific_SST_Monitoring
  website](https://ios-osd-dpg.github.io/Pacific_SST_Monitoring_Site/buoys.html). This
  complements pacea, which is suited for doing specific plots and
  analyses defined by the user.

## Calculations and plotting

### Default plot

We can easily calculate a climatology (by month) and subsequent anomalies for
each buoy, and plot results:
```{r, buoyanomalies}
all_buoys_anomalies <- calculate_anomalies(buoy_sst)

plot(all_buoys_anomalies)
```

The plot's title describes that this plot is for the anomalies **in April** (the
default) for all
buoys, and the climatology was 1991-2020 where
available. Buoys are arranged in a roughly north-to-south order (see map). So each square
gives the SST anomaly for that buoy for April of that year. Empty (white)
squares indicate not enough data available for that particular calculation.

The figure clearly shows that April 2015 and April 2016 were warmer than usual
for April, for every buoy (with those years having the warmest two Aprils for
almost every buoy). The bottom three buoys clearly have limited data; in
particular the anomalies in 2020 for both Entrance English Bay and South Georgia
Strait are 0, because the climatology for 1991-2020 only includes the value for
2020. 

### Absolute SST's

To show the actual monthly average SST's (rather than anomalies), again for the
default month of April:
```{r, buoyanomalies3}
plot(all_buoys_anomalies,
     sst_plot = "mean")
```
Here you can roughly see the water getting warmer from north to south, noting
that the three "NOMAD" buoys are much further offshore than the others, and
look slightly cooler.

### Full results for a specific buoy

If you specify a buoy, you get the monthly anomalies across the years (again
with an automated title), with months running from top to bottom:
```{r, buoyanomalies2}
plot(all_buoys_anomalies,
     stn_id = "Halibut Bank")   # In the Strait of Georgia
```

You can check that the April 2016 high anomaly matches that shown in the first
anomaly plot shown above.

### Anomalies for all buoys for different months

You can specify a single month (the default being "4" for April):
```{r, buoyanomaliesmonth}
plot(all_buoys_anomalies,
     months = 12)
```

Interestingly, in 2023 the December anomalies are all positive, whereas in the
first anomaly plot above the April anomalies are all negative (for the available
buoys in each case). Discuss. (We may use this example in future vignettes for
future plots; stay tuned).

If you specify multiple consecutive months (e.g. `4:6`), then the plot shows the anomalies
averaged over those months (and the title is automatically correct):
```{r, buoyanomaliesmonths}
plot(all_buoys_anomalies,
     months = 4:6)
```

The eagle-eyed amongst you will have spotted that the S. Georgia Strait buoy
does not appear on this plot (it was second from bottom in the previous
plots). We will come back to this later (briefly, the plot requires every
specified month in `months` to have an anomaly available, else it shows a blank).

And if you want a wintertime-ish (not strictly 'winter') index that includes December, that can be done:
```{r, buoyanomaliesmonths2}
plot(all_buoys_anomalies,
     months = c(12, 1, 2, 3))
```

As stated in the title, the year on the x-axis is the year of the January.

If you specify `months` and a single buoy, the anomalies for those months are
all shown individually:
```{r, buoyanomaliesmonths3, fig.height = fig_height_four_row_heatmap}
plot(all_buoys_anomalies,
     months = c(12, 1, 2, 3),
     stn_id = "Halibut Bank")  
```

This plot can be used as a check to see what anomalies are available (if you are
only interested in a particular buoy). It also shows explicitly that Dec-Mar is
missing at least one month in 1993 (i.e. Dec 1992 - Mar 1993) and 1994, but has
all four months available for 1995. That is why in the plot above that one,
"Halibut Bank" has no anomaly shown for 1993 or 1994, but does for 1995. 

### Returning the values shown in the plot

Setting `return_results = TRUE` returns a list containing the plot and then the
results used for the plot (and also automatically shows the plot). Repeating the
previous plot with this setting:

```{r, buoyanomaliesmonths4, fig.height = fig_height_four_row_heatmap}
res <- plot(all_buoys_anomalies,
            months = c(12, 1, 2, 3),
            stn_id = "Halibut Bank",
            return_results = TRUE)  
res$results
```

So `res` is a list (`res$plot` will show the above plot again), and
`res$results` is a tibble that includes the values
in the plot, as `sst_plot_value` and then `label` for the rounded values that are shown
numerically. You can then use these for analyses if desired.

That tibble contains results that depend on options used in the plotting. But we
will now examine the full results generated at the very beginning in
`all_buoys_anomalies`.

### Examining the climatology and anomalies

At the beginning we ran
```{r, alreadyrun, eval = FALSE}
all_buoys_anomalies <- calculate_anomalies(buoy_sst)
```

which we have plotted using various options. We now examine
`all_buoys_anomalies` in detail:

```{r, buoyanomaliesdetails}
all_buoys_anomalies
```
This is a list object, with `$climatology` giving, for each buoy and month, a mean SST
(`clim_sst_mean`), standard deviation (`clim_sst_sd`), and sample size
(`clim_sst_n`) of the values used for that buoy-month combination.
The default for `calculate_anomalies()` creates the monthly climatology for each
buoy based on the years 1991-2020 (details of other arguments will be
investigated later).

The `$anomalies` tibble gives, for each buoy-year-month combination, the anomaly
for that month compared to the climatology. The first buoy shown is "C46184"
which is the `r buoy_metadata$name[match("C46184", buoy_metadata$stn_id)]`
buoy. For October 1987 the mean SST was 10.1 degC (`sst_mean`), which was
calculated from 29 days (`sst_n`) in that month. The resulting anomaly from the
climatology is -1.16 (`sst_anomaly`). This can be manually checked -- the
climatology for buoy C46184 in October is a mean SST of 11.3 (the top tibble),
the mean SST in October 1987 was 10.1, which is -1.16 less (`sst_anomaly`). This
should help you understand how calculations are done. 

So the same calculations are done for all buoy-year-month combinations. There
happen to be a few NA's early on in the data for this buoy (more on that later).

The vector `$climatology_years` gives the years prescribed for the
climatology in the `calculate_anomalies()` call, for which the default is `1991:2020`.

The attribute shown (under `attr(, "class")`) given just tells R to use our customised plotting
function on these results, which is automatically called with `plot()`.

## Further calculation and plotting options

The `calculate_anomalies(buoy_sst)` uses the function
`calculate_anomalies.pacea_buoy(buoy_sst)`, which has further arguments that
users can tweak. See `?calculate_anomalies.pacea_buoy(buoy_sst)` for details,
but briefly these allow users to change:

- years used for the climatology period
- months and years to return anomalies for (defaults to all months and
years)
- minimum number of daily SST values required in a month for that month to be
  included in climatology calculation and anomalies calculation; defaults to 15
  days per month
- maximum number of consecutive days allowed to be missing (NA) within a
  month. If a time period has more than this many consecutive NAs, it is
  excluded from climatology and anomalies calculation; defaults to 6 days.

We (Elise Keppel and Andy) pragmatically decided on requiring 15 days (roughly half) of daily SST within
a month, and a maximum consecutive number of missing days of 6. This avoids
having, say, 15 days of data but all at the beginning of the month -- they need
to be somewhat spread out.
These are the
defaults, but can be changed to any number, or `NULL` to allow
all data and then examine the results for plotting.

The resulting `plot(all_buoys_anomalies)` uses
`plot.pacea_buoy_anomalies_list(all_buoys_anomalies)`, which also has arguments
that users can tweak. See `?plot.pacea_buoy_anomalies_list` for details, but
briefly these allow users to change:

- main title and axis labels
- whether to use the name of the buoy (e.g. `Middle NOMAD`) or the `stn_id`
  (e.g. C46004), by setting `use_stn_id_name` to `TRUE` or `FALSE`, respectively.
- whether to plot monthly anomalies, mean absolute SST values for each month, or
  counts of daily SST values used to calculate the monthly means; see below for
  examples, plus options to change the colour scale when plotting counts.

Decide what to keep:

- sst_plot character, one of:
  - `"anomalies"` (default) - plots SST anomalies
  - `"mean"` - plots mean SST values for each month
  - `"count"` - 

- `count_breaks` numeric vector of break points for the count plot colour scale.
 Only used when `sst_plot = "count"`. Default of `NULL` actually defaults to
 `c(0, 10, 15, 20, 31) * length(months)` if `months` is specified, else it is
 `c(0, 10, 15, 20, 31)`.

- `return_results` logical, if `FALSE` (default) returns the plot object only.
If `TRUE`, prints the plot and returns a list with both `plot` and `results`.

- `require_requested_months` numeric, number of months that must be available
out of the requested `months` to compute an average anomaly. If `NULL` (default),
defaults to `length(months)`. Only used when `length(months) > 1` and
`length(stn_id_to_plot) > 1`.
- `scale_limits` numeric vector of length 2 specifying the limits for the colour scale.
If `NULL` (default), limits are calculated automatically based on the data. Only used
 for non-count plots. If any plotted values are outside of `scale_limits`   then
 they are coloured grey.
 
`heatmap_colours` numeric vector of colours to use for the heatmap.
 Default is `pals::ocean.balance(20)[2:19]`, which provides 18 colours.

We suggest the following workflow if users want to tweak those defaults
(explained in detail below):

- do the calculations with the defaults (as above)
- plot the counts (number of daily SST values used to calculate the climatology
  and anomalies) 
- check if that looks satisfactory, both in terms of calculating the climatology
  and for doing the anomalies. Hard to automate, so just have to inspect
  manually (e.g. not too many big gaps).
- rerun `create_anomalies()` with a different `min_days_per_month` value, maybe
  also `max_consecutive_missing_days`.

The `sst_plot = "counts"` setting shows how many daily counts are available to
calculate each anomaly over the defined period. Say we want to look at the North
NOMAD buoy over Dec-Feb, we would plot the counts for those three months:
```{r, buoyanomalycounts, fig.height = fig_height_three_row_heatmap}
plot(all_buoys_anomalies,
     stn_id = "East Dellwood Knolls",
     sst_plot = "count",
     months = c(12, 1, 2))
```
So every month here has SST values for at least 16 days. Say we wanted to
instead insist on having 25 days of values for each month, we could plot the
same figure with a different colour scale:
```{r, buoyanomalycounts2, fig.height = fig_height_three_row_heatmap}
plot(all_buoys_anomalies,
     stn_id = "East Dellwood Knolls",
     sst_plot = "count",
     months = c(12, 1, 2),
     count_breaks = c(0, 25, 31))
```
which shows the months that would get dropped if we used the more stringent
criteria of 25 days per month. We can apply this criteria by recalculating the climatology
and anomalies:
```{r, buoyanomalycounts3, fig.height = fig_height_three_row_heatmap}
all_buoys_anomalies_require_25_days <- calculate_anomalies(buoy_sst,
                                                           min_days_per_month = 25)
plot(all_buoys_anomalies_require_25_days,
     stn_id = "East Dellwood Knolls",
     months = c(12, 1, 2))
```
Plotting the same figure with the default criteria of 15 days for each month, we
can see the extra months that get calculated (e.g. Dec 1989, Feb and Dec 1994):
```{r, buoyanomalycounts4, fig.height = fig_height_three_row_heatmap}
plot(all_buoys_anomalies,
     stn_id = "East Dellwood Knolls",
     months = c(12, 1, 2))
```

The extreme case of using all available data would be `min_days_per_months = 0`
  and `max_consecutive_missing_days = 32` in `calculate_anomalies()`, though
  this is not recommended (but can be used to check the upper limit of how much
  data is available).
  
Also, if a user wants to look at average SST for a buoy over the months
Jan-Jun, a decision has to be made as to how many months should be
available. 

We can also change the number of required months for a plot that averages of
multiple months.
Above, we noted that the S. Georgia Strait buoy does not appear in this plot:
```{r, buoyanomaliesmonths46}
plot(all_buoys_anomalies,
     months = 4:6)
```
This is because it does not have a climatology for Jun
therefore we cannot do a mean climatology for Apr-Jun:

```{r, noclimatology}
all_buoys_anomalies$climatology %>%
  filter(stn_id == "C46303") %>%
  a()
```
and the anomalies for 2022 (as an example) are:
```{r, noclimatology2}
all_buoys_anomalies$anomalies %>%
  filter(year == 2022,
         stn_id == "C46303") %>%
  a()
```
where you can see that Jun and Jul have SST values, but no anomaly because there
is no climatology for those months for this buoy (due to limited data, and the
default climatology years of 1991-2020). 

However, if we specify that we only require `require_requested_months = 2` months to be available to make a
climatology and anomalies for Apr-Jun
```{r, buoyanomaliesmonths46needless}
plot(all_buoys_anomalies,
     months = 4:6,
     require_requested_months = 2)
```
there are enough values, and so anomalies for this buoy can be calculated, but
beware that they are not truly anomalies that cover all of Apr-Jun.

Given the huge number of options that users may wish to explore (many buoys,
many years, many possible combinations of months), users may wish to relax or
tighten the defaults, and have the power to do so.
